acceptors_ is a member whose size is unmodified by any shown statement; the modulo in line 24 keeps the index within [0, size-1] whenever size >= 1.
routingPipelines_ map values are non-empty pipeline smart pointers, so a found iterator (line 6 admitted set) dereferences validly at lines 11-12.
childPipelineFactory_->newPipeline (lines 35-36) is treated by its name-implied semantics as returning a usable pipeline; no failure return is consumed in the fragment.
limitations: Line 24 (acceptors_[hash % acceptors_.size()]) would divide by zero if acceptors_ were empty, but no shown statement derives or can produce an empty acceptors_; per degenerate-input discipline this is not a finding.

Line 33 guard DCHECK(routingHandler) is debug-only; in NDEBUG a NULL routingHandler could be passed to newPipeline (lines 35-36), but no dereference of it occurs inside the fragment, so no NULL dereference is demonstrable here.

The cross-thread handoff of the detached socket (later fixed in wangle by deferring via originalEvb->runInLoop) depends on unshown DelayedDestruction guard-count and callback-context invariants; not confirmable from the fragment.
Raw allocation at lines 38-39 and acceptor/connection lifetimes are managed by unshown owners (ServerAcceptor::addConnection), outside the fragment's demonstrable control.

verdict.summary: Integer overflow in the data_size accumulation at line 92: width=2147483647, cpp=2, height=1 (all admitted by the guards at lines 83-85 and 87-88) give offset=4294967295 and data_size=8, so 'data_size += image->height * offset' wraps 8+4294967295 to 7. The wrapped data_size is consumed as the size argument of CreatePixels (lines 115-116) and CreateExtensions (lines 120-123), leaving a ~39-byte pixel area instead of the required ~4.3 GB (width*cpp+1 per row), causing an out-of-bounds write. The protective bound check (e.g. 'if (data_size >= UINT_MAX - image->height * offset) return (XpmNoMemory);') is absent from the fragment.

evidence.reason: Witness: image->width=2147483647, image->cpp=2, image->height=1, ncolors=0, ext_nlines=0. Line 81 computes offset=4294967295 (exact); the guard at lines 83-85 admits it (4294967295 > 2147483647 and > 2), the guard at lines 87-88 admits height=1 (1 < UINT_MAX/sizeof(char*)=536870911), so at line 92 data_size=8 plus image->height*offset=4294967295 gives 4294967303 which wraps mod 2^32 to 7. No bound check protects this addition (the required 'if (data_size >= UINT_MAX - image->height * offset) return (XpmNoMemory);' is absent). After line 98 data_size is ~39 bytes, while one row needs width*cpp+1=4294967295 bytes; line 115 passes data_size-header_nlines (~38) as the size argument to CreatePixels and line 121 passes the undersized area to CreateExtensions, which write the pixel strings (name-implied semantics: width*height rows of up to cpp chars plus newline) into that tiny region, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write. Primary CWE-190 integer overflow at the shown addition; secondary CWE-787 OOB write.

assumptions: XpmImage width/height/ncolors/cpp are unsigned 32-bit values; the fragment computes with unsigned arithmetic and compares against UINT_MAX, so the residual ranges in Phase 1 follow from the shown guards.
width, height, cpp and ncolors originate from a parsed XPM image (attacker-influenced library input); the fragment places no tighter visible cap on width/cpp beyond the lines 83-85 check.

Lines 84, 91, 93 and the duplicate assignment at line 94 are reproduction artifacts: interpreted literally as unconditional returns they would make lines 92-126 (including *data_return=data and ErrorStatus=XpmSuccess at lines 125-126) unreachable dead code, contradicting the task premise of a real paired function; the operative control flow reaches line 92 onward.
limitations: The allocation of the 'data' buffer is not shown in the fragment, so the destination capacity for the final OOB write is inferred from the shown data_size consumption at lines 115-116/120-123 per call-site confirmation semantics rather than a quoted declaration line.
CreatePixels/CreateExtensions bodies are unshown; their return values are discarded (lines 115, 120), which is a secondary status-handling concern but not independently confirmed.

The fragment never initializes or allocates 'data' (declared at line 9), making lines 102/107-108/112 use an indeterminate pointer; under the literal artifact reading those lines are unreachable, and under the intended reading the allocation is assumed present, so no separate CWE-457 finding is asserted.

If lines 91/93 were treated as real unconditional returns rather than artifacts, the reachable code would be bounded and fail-closed (function always returns XpmNoMemory); that reading would not make line 92 a reachable sink but contradicts the fragment's own final success assignment.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled info_content (argv[2]) is stored into the response header map with CR/LF intact because the sanitize_input call at line 44 is commented out; a value such as "en\r\nX-Injected-Header: 1" survives to the header map store at line 46 and enables HTTP response header injection (CRLF injection) when the map is rendered into response headers.

evidence.reason: The value stored at line 46 is sanitized_content, an unsanitized copy of info_content (line 43) whose provenance is the entry-point argv[2] (line 92). The protective sanitization call sanitize_input(sanitized_content); is present only as a comment at line 44 and never executes, so no transformation removes the CR/LF bytes and they survive to the sink. The map is documented as a response header map (docstring lines 14-16), so a witness argv[1]="lang", argv[2]="en\r\nX-Injected-Header: 1" passes the guard at line 38 (type_index=0 from lines 31-34) and injects a new HTTP response header, confirming CWE-113 HTTP response header injection via missing CRLF neutralization. The absent fix statement is the executed sanitize_input(sanitized_content); call.

assumptions: The type_to_key and header_keys arrays each have exactly 3 elements (lines 26-27), so num_types=3 (line 28) bounds type_index to 0..2 once the line 38 guard passes.

The header map is consumed by the enclosing program to build real HTTP response headers, as stated in the function docstring (lines 14-16) and by the presence of the CR/LF-stripping sanitize_input helper (lines 7-10).
limitations: The actual HTTP serialization that converts the map into wire-format headers is not shown in this fragment; if the map were only consumed by print_header_in_python_format (lines 74-83), the CRLF would only affect console output. This reliance on the documented response-header semantics limits confidence to 0.74.

parse_header also inserts attacker-controlled keys and values into the same header map with no CRLF sanitization (lines 55-67); it is a second path to the same injection class but is not treated as a separate finding.
The array indexing header_keys[type_index] at line 46 is safe: type_index is confined to 0..2 by the loop bound (line 31) and the type_index == -1 guard (line 38); no OOB candidate was confirmed.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart. main restricts msg to at most 255 characters (L47), generate_receive_log writes through size-bounded snprintf into a 296-byte allocation (L27, L34), and the allocation result is NULL-checked (L28). The format prefix at L34 is 32 bytes: '[' + 19-char timestamp + '] Received: '.

HTTP header termination is achieved only by CR and/or LF, both of which sanitize_input erases at lines 8-9.
std::map::operator[] at line 46 is a standard map insertion/lookup with no size constraint on the container.

parse_header stores attacker-controlled key/value pairs from argv[3] at line 67 without sanitization, but they only reach std::cout at line 77, which is not a security-relevant log/response sink in the shown fragment.
parse_header unconditionally returns true (line 70), making the failure branch at lines 96-99 unreachable; the dead status check has no security consequence.
No external caller invariants were assumed; all bounds derive from lines 26-28, 31, and 38.

verdict.summary: strncpy into sockaddr_un.sun_path uses sizeof(remote.sun_path) as the bound, so an endpoint name of length >= 108 leaves sun_path without a NUL terminator; the subsequent AF_UNIX connect() reads the path as a C string, over-reading past the 108-byte array.

evidence.reason: pipePath is the unconstrained return of endpoint.name() (line 4); line 11 strncpy(...) copies exactly sizeof(remote.sun_path) bytes, so any name of length >= 108 (the named capacity at line 11) leaves remote.sun_path unterminated. No guard on the path constrains pipePath length, so the witness passes lines 17, 44, 52, and 82, all of which are evaluated after or independent of the copy. connect() at this line consumes sun_path as a NUL-terminated AF_UNIX path, reading past the end of the 108-byte array into adjacent memory (CWE-125). The absent fix is an explicit terminator, e.g. remote.sun_path[sizeof(remote.sun_path) - 1] = '\0', or copying sizeof(remote.sun_path) - 1 bytes.

assumptions: remote.sun_path has the standard POSIX sockaddr_un fixed size used by sizeof at line 11.
AF_UNIX connect() treats sun_path as a NUL-terminated C string per its standard semantics.
FATAL_FAIL aborts on invalid fd results from socket()/close()/getsockopt(), as implied by its name.
limitations: endpoint.name() provenance is not shown; the length >= 108 input must be supplied by an unshown caller.
Exact extent and content of the out-of-bounds read depend on kernel/stack layout, not visible in the fragment.
The discarded select() return status (line 42) is a robustness/status-handling concern with no demonstrated security consequence and is not a finding.

verdict.summary: Unbounded strcpy copies endpoint.name() into the fixed-size sockaddr_un::sun_path buffer with no length check, letting an overlong pipe path overflow the stack buffer.

evidence.reason: pipePath originates at line 4 from endpoint.name() and retains the full string domain because no shown statement constrains its length before the sink. The destination sun_path is the fixed-size member of sockaddr_un remote; declared at line 5 (platform ABI capacity, 108 on Linux / 104 on macOS). strcpy writes strlen(pipePath)+1 bytes, so any pipePath with length >= sizeof(sun_path) overflows; the straight-line path lines 4->11 has no guard (no length check, no strncpy/snprintf, no truncation), and the absent fix is a length check or bounded copy before line 11. This is a confirmed stack-buffer overflow via unbounded copy, CWE-121.

assumptions: sockaddr_un::sun_path is a fixed-size char array per the platform ABI (108 bytes on Linux, 104 on macOS/BSD); the exact numeric capacity is not printed in the fragment.
strcpy writes strlen(src)+1 bytes including the NUL terminator.
limitations: The caller provenance of endpoint is not shown; exploitability requires the caller to pass a name of length >= sizeof(sun_path), which no fragment-internal constraint prevents.

dir_path itself is also user-supplied in the shown caller, which weakens the sandbox, but the missing filename/path-containment validation is still a confirmed CWE-22 under the function's stated contract.
No memory-safety (OOB/NULL/integer), format-string, or command-injection sinks exist in this fragment.

verdict.summary: The containment check at line 38 tests only whether the file's real path starts with the directory's real path as a raw string prefix, without a path-component boundary ('/' or equality) check. A filename such as "../dir2/secret" with dir_path "/tmp/dir" resolves to "/tmp/dir2/secret", which still satisfies the prefix test (string::find returns 0) and is then opened at line 43 and its content returned, allowing reads of files outside the intended directory.

evidence.reason: file_path (line 28: dir_path + "/" + filename) is attacker-controlled: filename retains its full string domain because no shown statement filters '/', '..', or path components (only realpath success at lines 22/32 is required). The security-decision guard at line 38 ('file_realpath_str.find(dir_realpath_str) != 0') admits a superset: it enforces a raw string prefix, not a path-component boundary, so the canonical sibling path '/tmp/dir2/secret' (from dir_path='/tmp/dir', filename='../dir2/secret') passes the guard (find returns 0) yet names a file outside '/tmp/dir'. The witness passes guards in order 22 -> 32 -> 38 -> 44 and reaches this open on line 43 and the content read at lines 49-52. The absent fix, which the vulnerable fragment is missing, is a boundary check such as requiring file_realpath_str[dir_realpath_str.size()] == '/' (or exact equality) after the prefix test. Primary CWE-22: path-containment bypass enabling read/disclosure of files outside the allowed directory.

assumptions: realpath() returns a canonical absolute path string on success (standard semantics, used at lines 22 and 32).
std::string::find returns the zero-based index of the first occurrence, so find(dir_realpath_str) == 0 tests only character-prefix equality (line 38).
dir_path must resolve for the witness (guard line 22), and the crafted target file must exist and be readable (guards lines 32 and 44), which the caller controls.
limitations: The demonstrated escape is limited to paths whose canonical string shares the directory's canonical string as a prefix (e.g., sibling '/tmp/dir2' or '/tmp/directory'); an arbitrary path such as '/etc/passwd' without that prefix is still rejected by line 38.
The exact filesystem layout (existence of the sibling directory and target file) is not shown in the fragment but is attacker-arrangeable via the two user-supplied arguments.
The realpath output buffers (lines 21 and 31) are not flagged: realpath fails with nullptr rather than overflowing an undersized buffer, and both failure returns are handled (fail-closed).

verdict.summary: In the NUV_EXTRADATA branch, the file-controlled size (line 13) is used to set extradata_size and to size an av_malloc call (lines 15-16), and get_buffer() (line 17) dereferences the unchecked allocation result with that size. When av_malloc(size) fails on a large attacker-chosen size, get_buffer writes through the NULL buffer, causing a NULL-pointer dereference/write (crash/DoS).

evidence.reason: Sink: get_buffer (standard avio-read semantics) writes up to 'size' bytes into the destination buffer. 'size' is the file-supplied le32 after PKTSIZE at line 13 with no in-fragment bound; the only path guard, line 14 (vst && subtype == 'R'), constrains neither 'size' nor the allocation result. The destination is the unchecked result of av_malloc(size) at line 16, a malloc-family NULL producer; capacity exists only if that allocation succeeded. Witness: frametype=NUV_EXTRADATA (line 8), subtype='R' (line 11), a large positive size (e.g. 0x0fffffff) at line 13, vst != NULL (admitted by line 14) passes lines 4-5, 6, 14 in order; on av_malloc returning NULL, line 17 writes up to 'size' bytes through the NULL pointer — CWE-476 NULL-pointer dereference. Absent fix: a NULL/return-status check after line 16 (e.g., if (!vst->codec->extradata) { vst->codec->extradata_size = 0; return AVERROR(ENOMEM); }). The equality check at lines 26-27 sits only in the NUV_MYTHEXT arm and never guards this path; line 18 post-dates the sink.

assumptions: get_buffer follows standard ByteIOContext/avio_read semantics: it copies up to 'size' bytes from the stream into the destination and does not NULL-check the destination.
av_malloc is a malloc-family allocator that returns NULL on allocation failure; its result is consumed un-checked at line 17.
The witness's vst != NULL is required by the fragment's own guard at line 14, so it is a guard-admitted value, not an external invariant; the sink path needs no constraint on ast or myth.
limitations: The allocation failure is an environment-dependent event (heap exhaustion / constrained platform), not a deterministic value; the attacker controls only the magnitude of 'size', which forces failure on constrained heaps.
PKTSIZE's definition is not shown, so the residual range of 'size' is stated as the file-supplied le32 with no visible in-fragment bound; the large-positive witness is admitted under any shown guard.
get_buffer's discarded short-read return (line 17) is treated as a robustness concern only — a short read cannot overflow the exactly-'size'-sized buffer at line 16.
url_fskip(pb, size) at lines 46/56 with attacker-controlled size affects only the file offset (possible negative/oversized skip), with no in-fragment memory consequence.
codec_get_id / wav_codec_get_id lookups with attacker-chosen tags are standard bounded-table lookups (unknown tags map to AV_CODEC_ID_NONE); no in-fragment failure demonstrated.
Line 15 stores the stale large extradata_size before the allocation; any downstream misuse of a NULL extradata with a large size occurs outside the shown fragment.

The element-node guard at line 83 admits this node and the strcmp dispatch at line 89 selects the 'name' branch; no NULL check exists between line 84 and this strdup, so strdup(NULL) dereferences NULL and crashes the process — CWE-476 NULL dereference. Absent fix: content != NULL check before this strdup.

The XPath literal //student always yields a node-set, so xpath_obj->nodesetval is non-NULL and nodeTab holds exactly nodeNr entries; nodeset->nodeTab[i] with i < nodeNr (line 75 vs 76) is in bounds, including the empty-set case nodeNr == 0.

No NULL-deref is reachable via nodeset->nodeTab: nodeNr == 0 skips the loop, and node-set entries are non-NULL per libxml2 invariants.

Memory leaks (unfreed xmlNodeGetContent buffers for name/age/citizenship, overwritten username/password contents, and the result struct when malloc fails at line 107) are robustness/DoS-minor concerns, not confirmed findings.
Plain free() on xmlNodeGetContent memory is safe under libxml2's default allocator; not assessed as a defect.

verdict.summary: write_results() generates the temporary file name with tmpnam() (line 21), which produces a predictable name in the world-writable temp directory without atomically creating the file, then opens it with fopen(filename, "w") at line 27, which follows symlinks. A local attacker can plant a symlink at the predictable name and cause the program to truncate/overwrite an arbitrary user-writable file or leak temporary contents; no mkstemp/O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW protection is present.

evidence.reason: Sink: fopen(filename, "w") opens the path produced by tmpnam() at line 21. tmpnam() is a documented legacy function that returns a name in the world-writable temp directory without atomically creating the file, and nothing in the fragment checks for a pre-existing entry or restricts symlink following (no mkstemp, no open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW), no lstat). The path from line 21 through line 22 (strdup) to line 27 is admitted by the only guard, line 21, whose tmpnam-NULL check merely confirms a name was generated. fopen with "w" truncates through an attacker-created symlink, so a local attacker who places a symlink at the predictable name can overwrite/truncate an arbitrary user-writable file (primary CWE-377 insecure temporary file; secondary CWE-59 link following). The absent protective statement is replacing tmpnam/fopen with mkstemp (or open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL plus fdopen).

assumptions: L_tmpnam (line 16) is the C-standard size sufficient for tmpnam()'s longest generated name, so the line-21 call cannot overflow tmp_name.

tmpnam() (line 21) is analyzed by its standard documented semantics: it returns a name in P_tmpdir (/tmp) but does not create the file, and its names are predictable/observable enough for a local attacker (superseded by mkstemp).
fopen(name, "w") (line 27) follows symbolic links and truncates the resolved target, per standard C library semantics.
limitations: Exploitability requires a local attacker able to predict/observe the generated name and plant the symlink within the tmpnam-to-fopen window; the exact predictability depends on the libc implementation, which lowers confidence.
The file is created with mode 0666 & ~umask and is never unlinked after use; disclosure of its contents to other local users is possible but secondary to the link-following issue.
The unused variable fd (line 18) is inert.
No memory-safety, injection, or status-handling flaw was found: strdup, fopen, fputs, and fclose return values are all checked (lines 23, 28, 33, 39).

Witness dir_path='/home/user', filename='../user_backup/secret.txt' passes guard line 21 (dir exists), line 31 (file resolves to /home/user_backup/secret.txt), line 36 (strncmp(...,10)==0 since byte 10 is '_'), is opened at this sink outside /home/user, and passes the NULL check at line 42, disclosing out-of-directory content. The absent one-statement fix is a boundary check that file_realpath[strlen(dir_realpath)] is '/' or '\0' (equivalently appending '/' to dir_realpath before the prefix test); the shown prefix-only test covers only non-prefix escapes such as ../../etc/passwd, so the failure set is not neutralized. Primary CWE-22: pathname is not properly limited to the restricted directory.

assumptions: filename and dir_path are attacker-controlled entry-point arguments (argv[1], argv[2]) after the argc==3 check at lines 68-70.
realpath output is canonical and NUL-terminated, so strlen(dir_realpath) is the exact canonical directory string.

The concrete witness requires an environment where a readable sibling directory/file exists whose canonical path begins with the directory's canonical name (e.g., /home/user_backup/secret.txt with dir /home/user).
Capacities relied on: file_path[1024] (line 26), dir_realpath[1024] (line 20), file_realpath[1024] (line 30) — none are exceeded by the demonstrated witness.
limitations: TOCTOU: fopen at line 41 uses the un-resolved file_path (line 27) after validation of file_realpath (lines 31-36); exploiting it additionally requires winning a race and mutating directory/symlink components (CWE-367), so it is not the primary finding.

Unchecked allocation failures: malloc(1) at line 18 and realloc at lines 51/59 would be dereferenced at lines 19/52/60 if they returned NULL, but no shown value or bound demonstrates allocation failure (CWE-476 not confirmable).

Unbounded per-byte realloc loop (lines 50-53) has no size cap; memory exhaustion is a resource concern, not a shown memory-safety failure.

AES_cbc_encrypt(
        padded_data.data(),
        encrypted_data.data(),
        padded_data.size(),
        &enc_key,
        iv_copy.data(),
        AES_ENCRYPT
    );
evidence.reason: The CBC encryption sinks the predictable IV: iv_copy (line 72) is a copy (line 64) of the hard-coded constant initialized at line 45, and no executed statement randomizes it; the RAND_bytes init/check at lines 47-51 is commented out, so the absent fix is an active random-IV initialization with return-status check. Residual range of key is size>=16 (guard line 37) but that guard is unrelated to the IV, leaving the constant IV admitted on every successful path to the sink. Every encryption under the same key with equal plaintext prefixes yields identical ciphertext prefixes, and with the fixed public IV a predictable-IV first-block attack applies, breaking CBC confidentiality (CWE-329).

assumptions: key.size() >= 16 before the line 42 iterator range is used, enforced by the throw at line 37.
AES_BLOCK_SIZE is OpenSSL's 16-byte constant, so padding_len in pkcs7_pad (line 14) is in [1,16] and AES_cbc_encrypt receives a multiple-of-16 length (line 70).

The observable impact of the fixed IV (key reuse, attacker seeing multiple ciphertexts) is the standard CBC threat model rather than a property established inside the fragment.
AES-128 key truncation and the hard-coded nature of the returned IV are by-design per the documented contract and are not themselves flagged.

The dlen guard (L37) only guarantees len <= dlen, and dlen counts tail->iov_len (L28), so admitted bytes need not correspond to filled page/vec entries. Resulting OOB write into rq_vec and OOB read of rq_pages (CWE-787, secondary CWE-125). Absent fix: a bound check such as 'if (v >= ARRAY_SIZE(rqstp->rq_vec)) return 0;' before the writes.

assumptions: rqstp->rq_vec and rqstp->rq_pages are fixed-size member arrays of struct svc_rqst, demonstrated by their subscripting at L44-L53 and L50; their exact capacities are not declared in the fragment.

limitations: The concrete sizes of rq_vec and rq_pages come from the unshown struct svc_rqst, so the witness is a range (len large enough that v exceeds those unshown capacities), not an exact single value; exploitability also depends on the receive path placing admitted bytes in head/tail rather than pages.
Whether the overflow yields only a crash or full memory corruption, and hence the remote-exploitation ceiling, is not determinable from the fragment alone.
The dlen check at L37, the count==len check at L20, and the max_blocksize clamp at L40-L42 were audited and do not bound v; they are insufficient protection, not demoted findings.

verdict.summary: On the PLATFORM_WEB branch, text is interpolated verbatim via TextFormat("%s") into a single-quoted JavaScript string and executed by emscripten_run_script without any escaping or validation, allowing apostrophe-based JavaScript injection.

The empty-string case (encrypted_pass == "") is handled safely by line 129's return RLM_MODULE_NOOP and is fail-closed, not a finding.

verdict.summary: The error paths of split() are unsafe: on failure of the final realloc, the fragment frees the working copy 'copy' a second time (already freed at line 20), a double-free (CWE-415); and on failure of the first realloc (result still NULL), the guard 'if (!tmp && result)' at line 8 evaluates false and control falls through to write result[0] through a NULL pointer (CWE-476). 'dupstr' returns a usable copy whose failure behavior is not shown and is not relied upon for either finding.

Integer overflow of '(i + 1)' at lines 7/23 would require more than 2^31 tokens (~4GB input) and is not a demonstrable in-fragment risk; not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: In the CD_FLAG_BIN branch, the problem-data item name is used unsanitized in concat_path_file(dd->dd_dirname, name) (line 78) and copy_file(value->content, dest, ...) (line 80). verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled mb_count from the packet header is only checked by log-only guards; when mb_count > left (line 20, 'COUNT ERROR' with no return), the decode loop at line 63 runs past the end of the mb_width*mb_height frame and MPV_decode_mb at line 80 writes out of bounds at row mb_y >= mb_height.

The only relevant guard, `if (mb_count > left)` at line 20, admits every value mb_count >= left+1 but merely logs (line 21) and does not terminate, so the loop guard at line 63 (`s->mb_num_left > 0`) executes all mb_count iterations. Witness: mb_width=mb_height=2, mb_x=mb_y=0 (passing lines 14-15), mb_count=5 -> left=4; after 4 in-frame iterations the wrap at lines 83-87 sets mb_x=0, mb_y=2, and iteration 5 reaches this line at row mb_height=2, outside the frame, writing past the heap frame buffer; with no SLICE_END (line 90) and decode errors only logged (lines 75-77), no exit prevents it. The absent protective statement is a termination (e.g., `return -1;`) after the line-20 COUNT ERROR check, and no other statement on the path bounds the iteration count; Fix-Scan found no covering guard. Primary mechanism: CWE-787 heap out-of-bounds write.

mb_count and s->mb_x/s->mb_y/s->mb_width/s->mb_height are populated by the header decoders from the packet bitstream initialized at line 6 from the entry-point buf, making mb_count attacker-controlled.

A decode-error result (ret != SLICE_OK) does not terminate the loop, so the overflow witness does not depend on the decoder succeeding at every iteration.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents is the fixed counterpart: the per-iteration bound check `if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;` (lines 53-54) covers every byte-swap sink, and dataLeft's word-aligned residual range (multiples of 4) makes the size==1 normalization consume exactly what the guard admits.

The request `length` is in 4-byte units (line 23 multiplies by 4) and `SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)` is 4-aligned, so dataLeft is a multiple of 4; every decrement at line 67 (`2*size` for size normalized to 1->2, 2, or 4) is also a multiple of 4, so the size==1 path (guard admits dataLeft >= 2, consumption 4) always actually has dataLeft >= 4 before consuming.
Lines 66-67 move `from.c8` and `dataLeft` strictly in lockstep, so dataLeft always equals the exact number of remaining bytes from `from.c8` to the end of the request.
limitations: The size==1 branch (lines 63-64) tests `dataLeft < 2` but consumes 4 bytes (lines 66-67); without the mod-4 invariant above, a malformed request with dataLeft == 2 or 3 and a higher set bit (e.g. bit 11, size 2) could underflow dataLeft and let a later iteration's `swaps` read past the buffer. Within the shown code that state is unreachable, so this is a robustness note only.
`ErrorF` at lines 70-71 formats the unsigned `dataLeft` as `%d`; a sign/type mismatch, cosmetic only, no injection because the format string is constant and the argument is numeric.

Whether the check at lines 53-54 is the exact statement introduced by the upstream fix cannot be confirmed from the fragment alone; the analysis relies on the guard's observable admitted/excluded sets.

verdict.summary: In parse_mb_skip, the SKIP_TYPE_COL (and SKIP_TYPE_ROW) remaining-bits guards only require 1 bit, but the else branches then read up to mb_height (mb_width) more bits via get_bits1 with an already-exhausted stream, permitting an out-of-bounds read past the end of the bitstream when exactly one bit remains and the skip flag is 0.

Absent fix: enlarge line 24 to get_bits_left(&s->gb) < s->mb_width + 1. Reads past the end of the available bitstream, CWE-125.

The size==1 branch (line 64 sets size=2) consumes 4 bytes after line 53 guaranteed only 2; with the demonstrated 4-byte-aligned dataLeft this is a protocol-consistency quirk with no memory-safety consequence, and the trailing 'if (dataLeft > 2)' (line 69) fails closed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. verdict.summary: classObjectOfPrivateScript() (line 4) can return an empty v8::Local when the private-script class lookup fails, and line 6 dereferences classObject->GetOwnPropertyDescriptor(...) with no IsEmpty/NULL check before the call, causing a NULL dereference (renderer crash). The missing fix is an empty-handle check such as "if (classObject.IsEmpty()) { ... }"/RELEASE_NOTREACHED() inserted before the dereference at line 6.

evidence.reason: classObject is produced at line 4 by the lookup classObjectOfPrivateScript(scriptState, className) and its residual range includes an empty v8::Local when the class is not found; no statement between line 4 and line 6 checks classObject.IsEmpty(), and the line 6 guard constrains only descriptor (and is evaluated at/after the deref), so an empty handle is admitted to the sink. Dereferencing through an empty Local calls Object::GetOwnPropertyDescriptor on a null Object* (V8 Local<>::operator-> yields nullptr for empty handles), a NULL-dereference crash (CWE-476). The absent fix is an added empty-handle/NULL check (e.g., if (classObject.IsEmpty()) ... RELEASE_NOTREACHED();) before line 6.

assumptions: scriptState and scriptStateInUserScript are non-NULL (no shown NULL producer).
className and attributeName are non-NULL internal literals; fprintf uses %s correctly (lines 7, 12).
V8 handle semantics: an empty v8::Local holds a null underlying pointer, so operator-> at line 6 yields nullptr.
classObjectOfPrivateScript is a fallible name-implied lookup whose result may be an empty handle when the private-script class is missing.
limitations: The body of classObjectOfPrivateScript is not shown; the empty-handle production is name-implied rather than demonstrated in-fragment. If that helper internally guarantees a non-empty result, the finding collapses — hence confidence is capped at 0.67.
No attacker-controlled trigger is shown for class-name lookup failure; impact assessed as medium (crash/DoS-class) rather than higher.

Sinks at line 11 (Cast(descriptor)) and line 18 (Cast(getter)) are fully guarded by the IsObject/IsFunction checks at lines 6 and 11, and result at line 23 is protected by the failure path at lines 18-21; these are not findings.

verdict.summary: The fragment contains the protective overflow check at lines 3-4: `if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;`. For every admitted (n, lb) pair, n*lb <= SIZE_MAX, so the unsigned multiplications at lines 21 and 26 cannot wrap. This is the fixed counterpart; no failure witness reaches either allocation sink.

`GC_malloc_uncollectable` and `REDIRECT_MALLOC` have standard allocator semantics: the result may be NULL on failure, and the fragment returns it without dereferencing.
limitations: The expansions of `REDIRECT_MALLOC`, `EXPECT`, and `GC_init_lib_bounds` are not shown, but none of them receive an arithmetic product that can exceed `SIZE_MAX` after the line 3 guard.
Allocation failure (NULL return) is a robustness concern governed by the caller contract, not a vulnerability demonstrable inside this fragment.

verdict.summary: The malloc-family result of g_strconcat (line 4) is stored in TypeInfo.name and passed to type_register (line 9) without any NULL/return-status check; on allocation failure ti.name is NULL and type registration dereferences/aborts on it, causing a NULL-pointer-dereference crash (DoS). The absent fix is a NULL check on the allocation result before registration.

evidence.reason: ti.name is assigned the result of g_strconcat at line 4, a glib malloc-family allocation whose standard residual range includes NULL on allocation failure; no NULL or return check exists anywhere on the path (the fragment has no conditionals), and the only consumer is line 9, type_register(&ti), whose name-implied standard semantics require a valid non-NULL type name and dereference/abort on NULL. The fragment lacks the neutralizing fix statement (e.g., 'if (!ti.name) return -1;' before line 9), so a NULL ti.name passes every (non-existent) guard and reaches the sink, yielding CWE-476 NULL-pointer dereference / assert abort (DoS).

assumptions: TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX and TYPE_MACHINE are compile-time constants, so lines 4-5 contribute only trusted, fixed strings.
g_strconcat follows standard glib semantics: it returns a freshly allocated NUL-terminated string, or NULL if the allocation fails (malloc-family).
type_register's standard, name-implied semantics require a valid non-NULL type name, which is dereferenced/keyed during registration; a NULL name cannot be registered safely.
m is a plain parameter with no in-fragment NULL producer, so m and m->name are treated as non-NULL per the plain-parameter rule.
limitations: The OOM precondition is an environment failure rather than a value derived from attacker-controlled input inside the fragment; impact is limited to crash/DoS, and confidence is calibrated down accordingly.
The exact internal dereference of ti.name occurs inside type_register, which is not shown; the failure relies on the name-implied standard semantics of type registration.

A NULL/empty or hostile m->name from an unshown caller is not confirmable from this fragment (no caller or producer is shown); no OOB is derivable because g_strconcat is length-safe for any non-NULL name and no capacity is declared.
The discarded return value of type_register is not a status-handling finding because QEMU-standard semantics abort on duplicate/invalid registration rather than returning an error.
ti.name is never freed; this is a one-time registration leak with no security impact in this context.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart of dbcs_ptr2len. The only security-relevant operation is the p[1] read on line 10, which is guarded by len == 2 and covered by the protective clamp 'if (len == 2 && p[1] == NUL) len = 1;' (lines 10-11): it never reports length 2 when the second byte is the string terminator, so a lone trailing DBCS lead byte cannot make an unshown consumer advance past the NUL. No capacity or NULL producer is visible in the fragment, so the p[1] read cannot be confirmed as out-of-bounds on any witness derivable from the shown statements.

assumptions: The fragment's own NUL tests (line 5 '*p == NUL' and line 10 'p[1] == NUL') evidence that p points into a NUL-terminated byte string, making p[1] readable (a data byte or the terminator) whenever the main path is entered.
MB_BYTE2LEN is assumed to return 1 or 2 for the DBCS encodings implied by the function name, so p[1] is the only byte past p that can be consumed.
The protective statement on lines 10-11 is the fix: it excludes the len == 2 && p[1] == NUL case from returning 2, clamping the returned length to 1.
limitations: An OOB read at p[1] (line 10) would require a caller-supplied unterminated or truncated buffer with no readable byte at p+1; no such object capacity is declared or derived in the fragment, and a claim based only on a missing upper-bound check is a limitation, not a finding.
NULL dereference of p on lines 5/9 is not confirmable because no NULL producer appears in the fragment.
Failure scenarios in unshown callers that consume the returned length were not assessable, since no call site is present in the fragment.

verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len reads p[1] whenever the first byte is a DBCS lead byte (len == 2 at line 8), with no check that a second byte is in-bounds. If p points at the final byte of a buffer, the p[1] evaluation reads one byte past the end (heap/stack over-read, CWE-125). The absent fix is a size/bounds check (e.g., 'len == 2 && (size < 2 || p[1] == NUL)') before reading p[1].

evidence.reason: p[1] is read as the right operand of the line-8 guard whenever len == 2, i.e., whenever *p is a DBCS lead byte (len = MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) at line 7). The guard admits every lead-byte value regardless of how many bytes remain at p; no shown capacity or remaining-length check bounds the read, and the p[1] == NUL comparison is the dangerous read itself, not a protector. Witness: p points at the sole byte of a 1-byte buffer whose value is a lead byte (0x91) — line 7 yields len = 2, line 8 evaluates p[1] one byte past the object (CWE-125 out-of-bounds read). The absent protective statement is an added bounds/size check (e.g., 'len == 2 && (size < 2 || p[1] == NUL)') before evaluating p[1]; line 9 only downgrades the returned length after the read has already occurred.

assumptions: MB_BYTE2LEN returns 2 for DBCS lead-byte values (e.g., 0x81-0xFE in cp932/cp936) and 1 otherwise, and examines only the first byte (*p).
The caller ensures *p (line 7) is a readable byte; the fragment unconditionally dereferences it.
limitations: The buffer's total capacity and the number of bytes remaining at p are not declared anywhere in the fragment; the witness 'only one byte remains at p' is a caller-supplied magnitude, which caps confidence at 0.74. If every caller guarantees at least two readable bytes whenever the first byte is a lead byte, the read is safe — that invariant is not derivable from the shown code.

Only a one-byte out-of-bounds read is demonstrated; there is no write-injection or other sink, so no memory-corruption/code-execution consequence follows from the read alone (crash or adjacent-byte disclosure).

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in rpmPackageFilesInstall: fdata is allocated with fc = rpmfilesFC(files) elements (L.15), but the payload-processing loop indexes it via &fdata[fx] (L.68), where fx comes from rpmfiNext() on the archive reader built from the attacker-controlled package payload (L.53, L.67). No shown check bounds fx by fc, so a payload whose cpio archive contains more entries than the header declares drives fx >= fc and the code writes through an out-of-bounds pointer.

evidence.reason: Sink &fdata[fx] with fx from the archive reader. Capacity: fdata = xcalloc(fc, sizeof(*fdata)) (L.15) with fc = rpmfilesFC(files) (L.10), valid indices 0..fc-1. fx is produced by rpmfiNext(fi) (L.67) where fi = rpmfiNewArchiveReader(payload, files, RPMFI_ITER_READ_ARCHIVE) (L.53) iterates the entry-point payload (L.4); nothing in the fragment ties the archive entry count to fc, leaving fx >= fc in the residual range. The loop guard (L.67) admits any fx >= 0 and precedes the sink; checks at L.49, L.56, L.63-64 do not constrain fx. The absent one-line fix is a bounds check such as 'if (fx >= fc) { rc = RPMERR_BAD_MAGIC; break; }' before L.68; without it, an archive with fc+1 entries makes fx = fc pass every guard and dereference one element past fdata (reads at L.70, writes at L.158) — confirmed heap out-of-bounds write, CWE-787.

assumptions: rpmfilesIter(files, ...) (L.23, L.55, L.168, L.182, L.203) yields exactly rpmfilesFC(files) indices 0..fc-1, because it iterates the same object whose count is read at L.10; this keeps the sinks at L.25, L.170, L.184, L.205 in-bounds.
xcalloc at L.15 never returns NULL (standard allocator semantics).
The branch at L.52 is entered with rpmteType(te) == TR_ADDED and fsmMkdirs (L.64) returns 0; both are shown branches and innocuous choices.
failedFile and the rpmts/rpmte/rpmfiles/rpmpsm parameters are non-NULL (plain parameters).
RPMFI_ITER_READ_ARCHIVE iteration of the payload's cpio entries is the only iteration driver not bounded by any shown statement.
limitations: The exact mapping of archive entries to returned fx values inside the unshown rpmfiNext/rpmfiNewArchiveReader is not visible; the finding rests on the absence of any in-fragment bound and on the payload being entry-point data. If an unseen rpmfiNext implementation clamped fx below fc, this overflow would not manifest — no such invariant is derivable from the shown code.
close(di.dirfd) with di.dirfd == -1 (L.161/L.17) is a robustness issue (EBADF), not a security finding.
No exploit of xstrdup / allocation-failure paths was evaluated.
Loops at L.169, L.183, L.204 were verified safe only via the same-object iterator assumption above.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown fragment. The only in-fragment arithmetic that can move the cursor line out of range, '++curwin->w_cursor.lnum' at line 35, is guarded at line 34 by 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count', which excludes the failing value ml_line_count + 1 before 'beginline(BL_WHITE | BL_FIX)' at line 36 reads the current line. FOR_ALL_WINDOWS(wp) at line 54 yields non-NULL window pointers, so wp needs no NULL check in the shown code.

verdict.summary: mov_read_stsz allocates sc->sample_sizes using 'entries * sizeof(long)' (L17) without bounding the attacker-controlled 'entries' value read by get_be32 at L10; on 32-bit size_t the product wraps to a tiny size, av_malloc succeeds, and the loop at L20-L21 writes entries elements far past the buffer (heap OOB write).

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787). entries comes unvalidated from get_be32 at L10 (residual positive range 0..2^31-1, attacker-controlled container bytes). At L17, 'entries * sizeof(long)' wraps to 4 on 32-bit size_t for the witness entries=0x40000001, so av_malloc returns a small block and the L18 NULL check passes; the L20 guard 'i < entries' admits every i up to 2^30, and each L21 write stores sizeof(long) bytes at offset 4*i, exceeding the wrapped allocation. Guard order on the path: L15 (admits sample_size==0), L18 (admits non-NULL undersized pointer), L20 (admits all positive entries). The absent protective statement is a pre-allocation bound check on entries (e.g., reject entries >= INT_MAX/sizeof(long)) that would exclude this witness; L18 only covers malloc failure and L15 only covers nonzero sample_size, so no shown guard covers the overflow failure set.

assumptions: ILP32 arithmetic for the wrap: size_t is 32-bit and sizeof(long) is 4, making the L17 product 'entries * sizeof(long)' wrap modulo 2^32 (the code base targets 32-bit builds where the multiplication type is unsigned 32-bit size_t).
av_malloc of the wrapped 4-byte size succeeds (alignment/padding adds at most a small constant) so the L18 NULL check does not trigger.
limitations: On 64-bit size_t (sizeof(long)=8), entries <= 2^31-1 gives entries*8 <= 2^34-8 with no wrap; the allocation would be enormous and normally fail at L18 -> return -1, and if it succeeded the loop would exactly fit, so the OOB is not demonstrated on that platform (only a possible resource-exhaustion concern, with no shown downstream consumer).
c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1] at L3 requires nb_streams >= 1; no shown statement establishes or violates that invariant, so it is not a finding.

uint32 entries values >= 2^31 truncate to negative int and are excluded by the L20 loop (only sc->sample_count becomes negative); downstream consumers of sample_count/sample_sizes are outside the fragment.

verdict.summary: The calloc fragment is the fixed counterpart: the overflow guard at lines 3-4 (`if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;`) is evaluated before both allocation sinks (lines 21 and 26) and excludes every (n, lb) pair whose product n*lb would wrap size_t, so the multiplication reaches the allocator only with a non-overflowing value.

This constant 0^32 salt is fed to PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC here (line 35), making every user's hash use the identical, publicly known salt: matching passwords hash identically across users and a precomputed table over the fixed salt covers the whole database. The absent fix statement is the uncommented "if (!RAND_bytes(hashed_passwords[i].salt, 32)) { ... exit(1); }" replacing the memset at line 31; primary CWE-338 (predictable/zero-entropy salt in the KDF).

When argc is even, a trailing username without a password is silently dropped by the (argc-1)/2 truncation at line 52; this is a fail-closed robustness concern with no demonstrable memory or authz impact.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability: every zlib buffer span is self-declared by the shown avail_out assignments (tmpblock capped at s->block_size * 3 at lines 13 and 30, deflate_block capped at s->deflate_block_size at line 20), src is NULL-guarded at lines 5-6, deflateInit and inflateReset failures are checked at lines 15-16 and 23-26, and no shown arithmetic exceeds a shown capacity.

assumptions: zlib inflate/deflate honor their declared avail_out/avail_in: inflate writes at most avail_out bytes and deflate consumes at most avail_in bytes, and both update avail_out only downward (standard name-implied callee semantics).

Each output span is self-declared in-fragment: tmpblock writes are capped at s->block_size * 3 (lines 13, 30) and deflate_block writes at s->deflate_block_size (line 20), so the intermediate produced-byte computations at lines 18 and 28 stay within [0, span] and cannot underflow.
s, s->tmpblock, and s->deflate_block are valid/non-NULL because no shown statement can produce NULL for them; their allocations are made outside the fragment.
limitations: A negative attacker-supplied `size` at line 11 would widen the uInt avail_in and over-read src, and a negative or overflowing `s->block_size * 3` at lines 13/30 would widen avail_out and overrun tmpblock; both require a producer of the bad value and a shown capacity for the target buffer, neither of which appears in the fragment (CWE-125/CWE-787 candidates demoted).

The return values of inflate at lines 14 and 31 and of deflate at line 21 are discarded; a failed inflate leaves partial tmpblock contents while the function still returns 0 at line 32, but any harmful use of that incomplete prime data happens in the unshown caller, so the status-handling concern (CWE-754) cannot be confirmed and is demoted to a robustness note.

Whether src, tmpblock, and deflate_block are individually large enough for size, block_size * 3, and deflate_block_size is established by allocation code outside the fragment and cannot be audited here.

verdict.summary: No demonstrated failing value reaches a security-relevant sink. The find_auth_end sentinel (line 43) is fully guarded by `if (auth_end >= 0)` (line 45), which excludes every negative value before the gssize-to-gsize store (line 48), the unsigned subtraction `buffer->pos - buffer->size` (line 49, which would wrap for a -1 'not found' sentinel stored as SIZE_MAX), and the g_bytes_new read at line 54; without that guard, a negative sentinel on a partial auth chunk would drive an out-of-bounds read. Reads are bounded by the shown 1-byte (line 14) and 64-byte (line 16) capacities, the failed-parse path is covered by `required < 0` (line 74), and the persistent current buffer is protected by the identity check at lines 22-23, so the fragment is the fixed counterpart.

assumptions: The auth-path buffer is the 64-byte allocation from line 16 (`else if (!client->authenticated) buffer = buffer_new (64, NULL)`), so buffer->pos is at most 64 because buffer_read consumes at most the buffer's remaining capacity (standard read-into-buffer semantics).

find_auth_end returns a negative 'not found' sentinel (standard -1) when the auth terminator is not yet in the buffer; this is corroborated in-fragment by the guard's form `if (auth_end >= 0)` at line 45.
buffer_new/buffer_unref/g_bytes_new follow GLib semantics: g_malloc-based allocations never return NULL, and g_bytes_new copies extra_data bytes starting at the given pointer.
side->current_read_buffer and side->header_buffer are initialized by the client setup outside the fragment; no statement inside the fragment can produce a NULL current_read_buffer.
limitations: find_auth_end's implementation is not shown; a hypothetical return in (pos, G_MAXSSIZE] would underflow line 49 and cause an out-of-bounds read at line 54, but no shown statement derives such a value, so it is treated as an unconfirmed residual range rather than a finding (CWE-125 would require a shown producer).

No cap on `required` from g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (lines 73, 81) is shown; a crafted D-Bus header could claim a large message size, but the header parsing and magnitude derivation occur inside GLib, outside the fragment.
A read failure at line 20 breaks the loop without setting side->closed; whether EOF can cause repeated callback invocations depends on the unshown buffer_read semantics.

The D-Bus header/body framing relationship (header_buffer capacity and how the body buffer of size `required` relates to the already-read header) is not shown, so framing-logic concerns are not assessed.

verdict.summary: Fixed counterpart: line 20's short-circuit guard (len >= strlen(signature_name)) fully protects isspace(signature_name[len]) (index evaluated only when len < strlen(signature_name), i.e., in-bounds), and the other shown hazards are neutralized in-fragment: NULL checks at lines 12 and 33, WTD_UI_NONE at line 45, and the exhaustive WinVerifyTrust status switch at lines 53-65. The message-resource formats MSG_283/284/285/240 are not shown; they are presumed fixed literals, so no format-string injection is confirmable.

The whitelist's prefix-plus-whitespace admission set is the intended design; acceptance still flows through WinVerifyTrust, whose non-success result is returned at line 67, so no signature-validation bypass is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed counterpart: lines 12-15 replace every single quote in url/title/description/feed_title with the literal bytes %27 before the command line is built (line 10) and dispatched to a POSIX shell on both paths (line 22 interactive, lines 26-31 /bin/sh -c). assumptions: Lines 27-28 hardcode /bin/sh, so a POSIX sh is the executor in which a single-quoted string terminates only at an unescaped ' (name-implied standard semantics of the exec at lines 29-31).
utils::replace_all (lines 12-15) replaces every occurrence of ' with the four literal bytes %27, which the shell does not re-interpret.
The format string at line 10 is a compile-time literal; strprintf::fmt uses printf %s semantics with c_str() arguments.
bookmark_cmd and is_interactive (lines 7-8) come from the user's own configuration and are treated as trusted.
limitations: A newline in a field survives the ' -> %27 sanitization and reaches the debug log at line 17, which could forge an additional log line (CWE-117); demoted because the log is the application's own debug output with no shown security/audit consumer.
If the executing shell were a non-POSIX variant with different single-quote semantics, the sanitization could be insufficient; /bin/sh semantics are assumed as shown.
Functionality note: the bookmark command receives the literal %27 sequence and must URL-decode it; this is a correctness concern, not a security one, in the shown code.

TtfUtil::LocaLookup follows the standard 'lookup with failure sentinel' semantics reflected by the fragment's own == size_t(-2) comparison at line 21 and the line 20 comment, i.e., an out-of-range glyph id returns the sentinel rather than indexing out of bounds.

Members _num_glyphs_graphics and _num_glyphs_attributes are unsigned short as implied by the zero initializers (lines 9-10) and the explicit cast at line 58; _num_attrs is uint16 as set from the read at line 39.

limitations: The bodies of Face::Table, TtfUtil::GlyphCount, and TtfUtil::LocaLookup are not shown; the safety of the line 21 lookup relies on the name-implied sentinel contract plus the fragment's own status comparison and comment, not on visible callee code.
Downstream consumers of _num_glyphs_attributes and _num_glyphs_graphics (outside this fragment) are not shown; within the fragment, all stored values are proven within their declared ranges.
The comment on line 50 questioning the 0x3000 attribute limit is a hardening/robustness note; it does not create an in-fragment memory, injection, or access-control failure.

A fail-closed edge exists: if the attribids array exactly fills the remaining Gloc bytes, tmpnumgattrs computes to -1 and the loader rejects the font; this is rejection of a legal boundary (robustness), not a security failure.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed counterpart: every dangerous operation is covered by a visible protective statement. The empty-match path is advanced by `pos++` (L113) so the match loop cannot stall; the one-byte copy at L111 is bounded by `if (pos < string_lim)` (L110), excluding the empty-match-at-end OOB read; the backref copy at L95-96 is bounded by the slice guard at L93-94 (`beg[n] >= 0 && beg[n] < end[n] && end[n] <= str.size()`); the nomatch tail copy at L118 is bounded by `string_lim - pos > 0` (L117); and the compiled-pattern NULL is checked at L50-52. No demonstrated failing value reaches an unguarded sink.

assumptions: Parameters pattern, replacement, str and option are user-supplied; String sizes are non-negative (`N = replacement.size()`, `S = str.size()`).
Oniguruma forward-search semantics: a returned match satisfies `beg[0] >= start`, so the prefix length at L80-81 is never negative (external invariant, not shown in the fragment).
`php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex` returns >= 1 for every byte (mblen-table lookup), so the replacement loop at L85 always progresses.
`enc != nullptr` is established at L21-22, and `syntax` is assigned on both branches at L31/L34.
limitations: Replacement-loop copy at L101 (`out_buf.append(p, fwd)`): if the last replacement byte were a multibyte lead byte, `fwd` could exceed `N - i` and read a few bytes past the logical end; this is demoted because it requires the unshown invariant that the active encoding (MBSTRG(current_mbctype), L20) is multibyte with width >= 2, and the extra reads land in NUL/terminator storage.

`pos` may momentarily advance one byte past `string_lim` via L113 after an empty match at the end; the next onig_search returns nomatch/error and the L117 tail guard prevents any out-of-bounds copy, so no failure is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: The 32-bit accumulator inc (line 3) is added to unconstrained int utility values over up to numCB iterations (lines 4-6) and can wrap; e.g., numCB=2 with utility[i]=2000000000 and error=INT_MIN, the line-5 product wraps yet still passes the > comparison, inc overflows at line 6 and the wrapped negative value is stored into utility_inc[i] at line 7. Upstream fixed this by widening inc/utility_inc to 64-bit.

evidence.reason: inc is declared int at line 3 (32-bit, initialized 0); utility[i] is an unconstrained int (no producer or bound shown). With numCB=2 and utility[0]=utility[1]=2000000000, the line-4 guard i < numCB admits i=1, the line-5 wrapped product (-294967296) is still > INT_MIN so the branch is true, and inc = 2000000000 + 2000000000 = 4000000000 wraps to -294967296 at line 6 (CWE-190), which is then persisted at line 7 (utility_inc[1]). No protective statement exists: no int64 cast, no saturation, and line 5 only gates whether accumulation occurs, not its magnitude. The absent fix is the one-line widening `int64_t inc = 0;` (with 64-bit utility_inc elements), per upstream FFmpeg commit 87ecefdab0097537c5c30014e57b19113ab05eee.

assumptions: Two's-complement wraparound semantics for signed int overflow (ISO C UB, but standard on FFmpeg's target compilers).
numCB, error, and utility[] are reachable inputs to this internal helper via unshown callers; they are unconstrained ints per the fragment, and the finding uses only in-domain values.
utility_inc is at least numCB int elements, required by the loop's own indexing contract at line 7 (capacity not shown in the fragment).
limitations: Out-of-bounds reads at lines 5-6 and the OOB write at line 7 are not confirmable: no capacity for utility/utility_inc is declared inside the fragment.
Any downstream OOB or logic consequence of the wrapped utility_inc (e.g., in get_high_utility_cell's modulus/index search) occurs in unshown code and is outside this finding.

verdict.summary: Every array access is bounded by the loop condition `i < elbg->numCB` (line 5), which admits only i in [0, numCB-1] and is the sole index derivation in the fragment; the accumulator `inc` is initialized to 0 as int64_t (line 4) before the loop, so no uninitialized or truncated accumulation is reachable. No capacity, type, or producer in the fragment demonstrates an out-of-bounds access or an integer overflow reaching a security-relevant sink.

assumptions: Loop semantics of line 5: `i < elbg->numCB` guarantees every admitted iteration has i in [0, numCB-1], and `numCB <= 0` skips the body entirely.
Line 4 (`int64_t inc=0;`) executes unconditionally before the loop in program order, so all reads of `inc` (lines 7-8) see an initialized value.
Array indices used at lines 6-8 are derived only from the loop counter `i`, never from any other fragment computation.
limitations: The element types of `elbg->utility` and `elbg->utility_inc` (and the type of `elbg->error`) are not declared in the fragment, so the product at line 6 (`elbg->numCB*elbg->utility[i]`) cannot be shown to overflow in the displayed types; no int-width overflow finding is confirmable.

No capacity for `utility` or `utility_inc` is declared or computed in the fragment; an out-of-bounds write at line 8 would require an unshown producer allocating fewer than `numCB` elements, which is not derivable from shown statements.
An int64 accumulation overflow at line 7 would require magnitudes (near-INT64_MAX values over many iterations) that no shown statement produces.
If the code pair's vulnerable counterpart had `int inc;`/`int inc=0;`, the shown `int64_t inc=0;` at line 4 is exactly the one-line fix that neutralizes the uninitialized/truncated accumulation.

verdict.summary: fill_table computes int64_t cb = av_clip(i-YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM, 0, 255)*inc (line 8) with inc declared as const int (line 2) and never validated. Both multiplication operands are int, so the product is computed in 32-bit signed int and overflows/wraps for any |inc| > INT_MAX/255 (e.g. inc = 2^24 with a clipped value of 255), producing a corrupted value that is consumed at line 9 as the pointer offset elemsize * (cb >> 16), storing an out-of-range LUT pointer. The upstream one-statement fix — declaring inc as int64_t — is absent; the int64_t cb declaration does not widen the int*int arithmetic.

evidence.reason: Signed 32-bit overflow (CWE-190): inc (const int, line 2) retains its full int domain because no fragment statement constrains it; av_clip returns int in [0,255], so av_clip(...)*inc is an int*int product computed in 32 bits before assignment to int64_t cb. Witness: i = 255+YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM admitted by loop guard at line 7 (i < 256+2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM), clip result 255, inc = 2^24 (admitted, unguarded) gives 255*2^24 = 4,278,190,080 which wraps to -18,714,816; the wrapped value feeds the consumer at line 9 (elemsize * (cb >> 16) = -286*elemsize), building a pointer outside the intended 256-entry table. The int64_t cb declaration does not neutralize the overflow (both operands remain int), and the absent fix statement is the upstream type change of inc to int64_t (FFmpeg commit a494792961a08f9f0e47e7eeed65e609178ff436).

assumptions: YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM is a positive constant, so i = 255+YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM satisfies the line 7 loop condition (255+2H-1 max index matches the line 1 declared table capacity).
y_tab and table point to valid objects of the sizes implied by the line 1 declaration; their actual allocations are outside the shown fragment.

Mainstream compilers use two's-complement wrap and arithmetic right shift, giving the concrete wrapped value -18,714,816 and offset -286; the claim (corrupted value consumed) holds for any conforming wrap behavior.
limitations: The magnitude of inc required to trigger the overflow (|inc| > INT_MAX/255 ~ 8.42e6) must be supplied by an unshown caller; real FFmpeg callers pass color coefficients around 1e5, so practical exploitability is not established from the fragment alone.
The line 9 pointer store and the downstream dereference (potential CWE-787/125) cannot be confirmed because the y_tab-backed allocation size is not shown; excluded from findings.
Line 6 (y_table -= elemsize * (inc >> 9)) performs unshown-bounds pointer arithmetic and implementation-defined shifts; demoted for lack of a shown capacity.
The line 9 table[i] write itself is safe: the line 7 '<' bound matches the line 1 declared capacity exactly with no off-by-one.

verdict.summary: This png_zalloc fragment is the fixed counterpart. The overflow bound check at line 14 (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) fully protects the items*size multiplication at line 19 from 32-bit wrap for every size > 0, the NULL check at lines 8-9 protects the p->flags dereference at line 12, the NULL check at lines 26-27 protects the png_memset calls in the PNG_1_0_X block, and the chunked zeroing at lines 31-33/37 is bounded by the allocation made at line 22. No demonstrated failing value reaches a dangerous operation; the only residual concern is the size==0 division at line 14, whose reachability is not shown.

assumptions: png_malloc honors the PNG_FLAG_MALLOC_NULL_MEM_OK flag set at line 21 and can return NULL, which the fragment checks at lines 26-27.

With size > 0, the guard at line 14 admits only items <= PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size, so items*size at line 19 is at most (PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size)*size <= PNG_UINT_32_MAX and cannot wrap; this holds whether uInt is 16- or 32-bit.
The two png_memset calls at lines 31-33 write exactly 0x8000 + (num_bytes - 0x8000) = num_bytes bytes, matching the allocation size passed to png_malloc at line 22.
limitations: Line 14 divides by size; a caller passing size == 0 would fault (SIGFPE). No shown statement in the fragment derives 0 for size (no call site is shown), so the degenerate witness fails the shown-code derivation requirement and the issue is demoted, not confirmed.

The cast (png_size_t)(num_bytes - 0x8000) at line 33 assumes png_size_t is wide enough for the chunk length; a narrower png_size_t would only under-zero the buffer (correctness), not write out of bounds.
png_malloc's internal behavior beyond the NULL-mem-ok contract is not shown and is out of scope.

verdict.summary: The option-parsing loop feeds argv-derived optarg to sscanf with an unbounded '%s' conversion into 10-byte stack buffers (cases 's', 'f', 'b', 'l'); any argument token of length >= 10 overflows the stack buffer, and longer argv strings overflow proportionally.

evidence.reason: optarg is argv-derived (getopt_long at lines 58-59, entry-point input) and the only guard is `if (optarg)` at line 92, which admits any non-NULL string of arbitrary length; no length cap narrows its residual domain. `%s` in the sscanf writes the input token plus a terminating NUL into dr, whose capacity is declared at line 94 as `char dr[10];`. A 10-character argument (e.g. `-s 0123456789`) writes 11 bytes, overflowing by 1 byte, and longer tokens overflow more. The `sscanf(...) < 1` test is evaluated after the write and protects nothing. The absent fix is a bounded conversion such as `"%9s"` or an explicit strlen check. This is a stack-based buffer overflow, CWE-121.

For case 'f', optarg (argv-derived at lines 58-59) passes the only guard `if (optarg)` at line 103 with no length constraint, keeping its full domain of arbitrary-length strings. The unbounded `%s` writes into dr declared `char dr[10];` at line 105; any >=10-byte token writes at least 11 bytes with the trailing NUL, overflowing the stack object. The return-value test at line 106 runs after the corruption. The missing fix is the width-restricted format `"%9s"`. Primary CWE is CWE-121.

For case 'b', optarg from getopt_long (lines 58-59) retains its full unbounded string domain past the only guard `if (optarg)` at line 117. The `%s` conversion writes the token and NUL into the 10-byte buffer declared at line 119 (`char dr[10];`), so a 10-byte argument overflows by one byte and longer inputs by more. The status check at line 120 executes only after the write and cannot prevent the overflow. The absent protective statement is a bound on the conversion, e.g. `"%9s"`. Primary CWE is CWE-121 (stack-based buffer overflow).

For case 'l', the argv-derived optarg (getopt_long at lines 58-59) passes `if (optarg)` at line 131 with no width/whitespace-length bound, so any non-NULL string is admitted. The `%s` conversion writes into the stack buffer declared at line 133 (`char dr[10];`); a token of exactly 10 characters writes 11 bytes including NUL, overflowing by one byte, and longer tokens overflow further. The `sscanf(...) < 1` test at line 134 is downstream of the write and provides no protection. The absent fix is the width-limited format `"%9s"`. Primary CWE is CWE-121.

assumptions: optarg is the argv option-argument pointer from getopt_long (lines 58-59) and is therefore entry-point/attacker-controlled; its only shown constraint is non-NULL.
sscanf '%s' writes the scanned token plus a terminating NUL with no implicit bound, per standard C semantics.
All four sinks are reachable during the parse loop at lines 38-173, which runs before the file-argument/showHelp checks at line 192.
limitations: The fread at line 262 discards its return value; for a file or stdin stream shorter than 8 bytes, header[4..7] are uninitialized and are consumed at lines 267 and 277-284. This is a potential CWE-457 uninitialized-use / robustness concern with no demonstrated memory-safety failure, so it is not counted as a primary finding.
The timing print at lines 308-309 divides by dec_length, which could be 0.0 if clock() does not advance; this is not security-relevant.
Format selection for file_ext[] (lines 226 and 239) is protected by the range check at lines 111-112 combined with the early return at lines 192-196, so that indexing path is not reported.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled command-line strings are copied with unbounded strcpy and unbounded %s sscanf into fixed 255-byte and 10-byte stack buffers, producing stack buffer overflows reachable from the option parser and the positional filename argument.

evidence.reason: optarg from getopt_long (line 58) retains its full unbounded length after the only guard, 'if (optarg)' at line 66, which is a NULL test only. strcpy writes strlen(optarg)+1 bytes into audioFileName, whose capacity is exactly 255 bytes declared at line 20 (valid indices 0..254). Witness: '-o' plus 300 'A's passes guards 61 and 66 and writes 301 bytes. The absent fix is a length check (e.g., 'if (strlen(optarg) < 255)') or a bounded copy before line 69. Primary CWE-121 stack buffer overflow (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write at the strcpy sink).

Same defect as line 69 for the '-a' option: the only guard is 'if (optarg)' at line 73 (NULL test), and strcpy writes strlen(optarg)+1 bytes into adtsFileName, capacity 255 declared at line 21. Witness: '-a' plus 300 'A's. Absent fix: length check or bounded copy before line 76. CWE-121/CWE-787.

For '-s', '%s' without a width writes the non-whitespace token plus NUL into dr, capacity 10 declared at line 82. Witness: '-s 1234567890' (10 chars => 11 bytes) passes guard line 80; the '< 1' return check on this same statement is evaluated only after the write and cannot bound it. Absent fix: width specifier '%9s'. CWE-121/CWE-787.

For '-f', identical unbounded '%s' write into dr, capacity 10 declared at line 93, guarded only by 'if (optarg)' at line 91. Witness: '-f 1234567890' overflows by 1 byte. Absent fix: '%9s'. CWE-121/CWE-787.

For '-b', identical unbounded '%s' write into dr, capacity 10 declared at line 107, guarded only by 'if (optarg)' at line 105. Witness: '-b 1234567890' overflows by 1 byte. Absent fix: '%9s'. CWE-121/CWE-787.

For '-l', identical unbounded '%s' write into dr, capacity 10 declared at line 121, guarded only by 'if (optarg)' at line 119. Witness: '-l 1234567890' overflows by 1 byte. Absent fix: '%9s'. CWE-121/CWE-787.

argv[optind] retains its full unbounded length: the only guard on the path, line 181 '((argc - optind) < 1) || showHelp', merely requires one remaining operand (optind <= argc-1) and showHelp==0; it does not bound string length. strcpy writes strlen(argv[optind])+1 bytes into aacFileName, capacity 255 declared at line 19. Witness: a 300-byte positional argument. Absent fix: length check or bounded copy before line 196. CWE-121/CWE-787.

assumptions: getopt_long supplies a non-NULL optarg for the required-argument options 'o','a','s','f','b','l' declared in the option string at line 58, so the 'if (optarg)' guards at lines 66/73/80/91/105/119 admit the witnesses.
argv strings are NUL-terminated and are not length-constrained anywhere in the fragment, so lengths exceeding 255 (and 10) are members of the admitted sets on the quoted paths.
limitations: Line 216 'strcat(audioFileName, file_ext[format])' can overflow for near-255-byte names (a 254-char operand with no '.' plus any non-empty extension), but the contents/length of file_ext[] are not shown, so the appended-size derivation depends on an unshown constant; it is not independently confirmed and inherits the same class as the line 196 overflow.

The fread return at line 239 is discarded; if fewer than 8 bytes are read, header[4..7] are uninitialized when compared at line 244 and pushed back through ungetc at lines 254-261 (CWE-457/CWE-754 potential), but no memory-safety or disclosure impact is demonstrable from the shown code, so it is not confirmed.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime forwards the unguarded src pointer into s->zstream.next_in (line 8) and passes it to inflate (line 12), which dereferences next_in while avail_in > 0; a NULL src (the caller-supplied block pointer, unconstrained in this fragment) causes a NULL-pointer dereference. The shown code is the pre-fix form of FFmpeg commit b6671787, whose one-statement fix 'if (!src) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;' is absent here.

evidence.reason: The uint8_t *src parameter (line 1) is stored into s->zstream.next_in at line 8 with no NULL test, and line 9 assigns the unvalidated size to avail_in; at line 12 inflate dereferences *next_in whenever avail_in > 0, so src == NULL with size > 0 yields a read at address 0 (CWE-476). No statement between line 1 and line 12 constrains src; the only guards, 'if (deflateInit(&zs, 0) != Z_OK) return -1;' (lines 13-14) and the inflateReset check (lines 21-24), run after the sink and check different operations, so they admit the witness. The protective statement covering the whole failure set, 'if (!src) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', is absent from the fragment (it is the one-statement fix in upstream commit b6671787).

assumptions: zlib inflate reads at most avail_in bytes from next_in and writes at most avail_out bytes to next_out; a nonzero avail_in with next_in == NULL dereferences NULL (standard zlib semantics).
s, s->zstream, s->tmpblock, s->deflate_block, and s->avctx are valid non-NULL (no in-fragment NULL producer); the stream was initialized by the decoder init outside the fragment.
avail_out only decreases from the configured block_size * 3 / deflate_block_size, so the differences at lines 16 and 26 are non-negative.
limitations: The concrete NULL provider for src (the same-revision caller flashsv_decode_block passes s->blocks[blk_idx].pos, an uninitialized block pointer) is not shown in the fragment, so the witness rests on the unconstrained pointer domain; confidence is therefore capped at 0.74.

Buffer capacities for s->tmpblock and s->deflate_block are not shown, so an out-of-bounds write via block_size * 3 or deflate_block_size, and the s->block_size * 3 signed overflow, are not confirmable.
Discarded return values of inflate (lines 12, 29) and deflate (line 19) with unconditional return 0 (line 30) are status-handling concerns with no demonstrable in-fragment security consumption.
A negative size widening into uInt avail_in at line 9 has unshown provenance and is not separately confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability: the fragment contains its own protective statements — the zero-length guard (lines 4-6), the ret>0 progress check (line 10), the outpos<outlen completion branch (line 13), and the paired outlen/outpos resets (lines 19-20). Together they preserve 0 <= outpos <= outlen on every path to the qemu_chr_fe_write sink, so no negative-length or out-of-bounds access is demonstrable from the shown statements.

qemu_chr_fe_write returns at most the requested length; it returns <= 0 when the backend is disconnected or not writable (name-implied standard semantics used for call-site confirmation).

The fragment's own transitions keep 0 <= outpos <= outlen at the send: label: outpos grows only by a positive ret (line 11), outlen/outpos are reset together (lines 19-20), and the reset back-edge sets outlen=2/outpos=0 (lines 31-32).
VM_CMD_RESET and VM_CMD_CHAR are compile-time constants.
